title: Object Types
summary: Object types describe the properties an object can have.

subtopics.title: Main idea
subtopics.explanation: A property has a name and a type, such as `{ title: string }`. The name identifies the field and the type describes its allowed value. It is like a labeled blank on a form. TypeScript can then catch code that assigns a number where a string is expected. For example, a product record can require an id and title while making a subtitle optional.

subtopics.title: Important part
subtopics.explanation: A `?` after a property name means that property may be absent, as in `{ nickname?: string }`. It is like an optional question on a form. Code must check for absence before using the value as a definite string. For example, a nested address shape can require city and country fields.

subtopics.title: How it works
subtopics.explanation: A `readonly` property should not be reassigned through the declared type. It is like a printed field that users can read but not edit. This restriction is checked by TypeScript and does not freeze the object in JavaScript at runtime. For example, mark an id readonly when callers should not reassign it through the declared type.

subtopics.title: A useful detail
subtopics.explanation: Nested object types describe properties that themselves contain objects. For example, a user can have an address with a city. It is like a form with a smaller address section inside it. Keep nesting understandable and name repeated shapes so they are easier to reuse. For example, a union can express a result that is either success data or a named error.

subtopics.title: Good practice
subtopics.explanation: Use an interface or type alias to name a shape used in several places. A shared name is like a standard form everyone on a team agrees to use. Keep the shape focused on the data contract, and add runtime validation when the data arrives from outside the program. For example, validate parsed server data before assigning it to a trusted object shape.

foundations.overview: An object type describes which named properties an object can have and the type of each value. TypeScript checks code against that shape while you develop. Think of it like a form template with named fields. Optional and readonly modifiers express additional rules, but these checks do not validate external data at runtime.
foundations.whyItMatters: Object types make assumptions about data visible and reusable. They help catch mistakes across components, while explicit optionality and runtime checks keep those assumptions honest.
foundations.browserPerspective: Object types are erased at compile time; the browser only ever sees plain JavaScript objects. There is no runtime shape enforcement — the safety is entirely in the compiler.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Typing React props (`interface Props { title: string }`), API response shapes, form state, configuration objects, and function options bags all rely on object types.
foundations.businessImpact: Catching shape mismatches at compile time prevents a whole class of runtime crashes (reading properties of undefined), reducing production incidents and support load.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Named object types document intent and give autocomplete, so engineers can refactor confidently — rename a field and the compiler points to every place that breaks.
foundations.performanceImpact: Zero runtime cost — types are erased. Very large or deeply nested object types can slow the type-checker and editor, so split big shapes into reusable named types.
commonUseCases: Typing React component props with an interface
Modeling API response and request bodies
Describe props shared between a page and its child component.
Model a form record with required and optional fields.
Name a nested API object used by several functions.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An object must match the type exactly, with no extra properties.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Structural typing allows extra properties — except excess property checks fire on fresh object literals assigned directly to a typed target.

commonMisconceptions.myth: interface and type are fundamentally different for object shapes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For plain object shapes they're nearly interchangeable; interface supports merging/extension while type can also express unions and primitives.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An object type checks values that arrive from the network.
commonMisconceptions.reality: TypeScript checks source code; runtime validation must inspect external values.
Readonly is shallow unless nested properties are separately protected, and it is not runtime freezing.

visualExplorer.title: How TypeScript checks an object against a type
visualExplorer.caption: Step through assigning an object literal to a typed variable and see how shape checking works.

config.intro: Trace assigning { id: 1, name: 'Ada' } to a variable typed as { id: number; name: string }.

steps.name: Declare the shape
steps.detail: interface User { id: number; name: string } names the contract: an id number and a name string.

steps.name: Write the literal
steps.detail: const u: User = { id: 1, name: 'Ada' } creates a fresh object literal targeting User.

steps.name: Check required members
steps.detail: TypeScript verifies id is a number and name is a string — both match.

steps.name: Run excess property check
steps.detail: Because it's a fresh literal, any property not in User (a typo) is flagged immediately.

steps.name: Accept by structure
steps.detail: The shape matches the contract, so the assignment is allowed — no name comparison needed.

interactiveExamples.title: Inline vs named object types
interactiveExamples.explanation: Both describe the same shape; the named interface is reusable and self-documenting.

interactiveExamples.title: Structural typing in action
interactiveExamples.explanation: An object with extra fields still satisfies a type that needs only a subset — duck typing.

hints: Use interface or type to name the shape.
Nest a braced object type for the customer property.

keyTakeaways: A property has a name and a type, such as `{ title: string }`.
A `?` after a property name means that property may be absent, as in `{ nickname?: string }`.
A `readonly` property should not be reassigned through the declared type.
Nested object types describe properties that themselves contain objects.
Use an interface or type alias to name a shape used in several places.
